title: Thermodynamics
summary: The first law is energy conservation with heat and work: $\Delta U=Q-W$. The second law says heat flows spontaneously hot → cold and no engine is perfectly efficient — engine efficiency is capped by the Carnot limit $1-T_c/T_h$.

second law.plain: Heat flows hot → cold; entropy rises.

concept_sections.heading: The first law
concept_sections.explanation: Energy is conserved: internal energy change equals heat in minus work out, $\Delta U=Q-W$. Watch the signs of $Q$ and $W$.
math_steps: Heat in is $+Q$; work by the gas is $+W$.

concept_sections.heading: Work in gas processes
concept_sections.explanation: As a gas expands it does work $W=P\Delta V$ (constant pressure) — the area under the $P$–$V$ curve.

concept_sections.heading: The second law
concept_sections.explanation: Heat won't flow cold → hot on its own, entropy tends to increase, and no engine converts heat fully to work.

concept_sections.heading: Heat engines
concept_sections.explanation: An engine absorbs $Q_h$, outputs work $W$, and rejects $Q_c$: efficiency $e=W/Q_h=1-Q_c/Q_h$.

concept_sections.heading: The Carnot limit
concept_sections.explanation: Between hot and cold reservoirs, the best possible efficiency is $e_{max}=1-T_c/T_h$ (kelvin). Real engines fall short.

real_world_examples.title: A gasoline engine
real_world_examples.scenario: Fuel burns to move a car.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Only part of the heat becomes work; the Carnot limit caps the best case.

real_world_examples.title: A refrigerator
real_world_examples.scenario: It moves heat from cold to hot.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: That requires work — the second law forbids it happening for free.

real_world_examples.title: A power plant
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Running hotter raises the Carnot efficiency, so plants push $T_h$ as high as materials allow.
